idiom_name: Enumerable#lazy with select/map/drop/take_while forced by first/force
implementation_notes: Ruby's lazy collection is Enumerator::Lazy: Enumerable#lazy returns a lazy enumerator over any Enumerable, so a chain such as (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy.select(&:odd?).drop(10).take_while { |i| i < 30 } performs per-element work only when a terminal method (first, force, to_a, each) demands it. Lazy chains are re-evaluated per enumeration and not memoized, so caching or Array materialization is the answer when the same elements are needed twice; the classic eager Enumerable pipeline stays simpler when the data fits memory and is traversed once.
code_sketch:
fib = Enumerator.new do |y|          # external iteration: nothing runs yet
  a, b = 0, 1
  loop { y << a; a, b = b, a + b }
end

evens = fib.lazy.select(&:even?).first(10)   # forces just enough elements
p evens
pitfalls: Lazy enumerators are not memoized: each enumeration re-runs the chain over the source, so an expensive lazy pipeline used twice must be forced once (force/to_a) or cached.
Holding a lazy enumerator keeps the source and every captured closure alive - a long-lived lazy chain over a large collection is a retention bug waiting to happen.

The lazy protocol depends on method names: only methods implemented by Enumerator::Lazy preserve laziness (select/map/drop/take_while...), and calling an eager Enumerable method mid-chain (sort, group_by, each_slice without lazy) silently materializes everything.

variants.name: External Enumerator driven by next
variants.idiom_name: Enumerator#next / Enumerator::Yielder as an explicit pull cursor
variants.implementation_notes: An Enumerator wraps any each-style method and exposes explicit external iteration: next pulls one element at a time (raising StopIteration at the end), peek looks ahead, and Enumerator.new { |y| ... } lets a producer push elements into the yielder exactly when the consumer asks, which is how the classic lazy generator is written in Ruby. Use it when the consumer needs index-like control or to interleave two sequences manually; the lazy chain variant is cleaner for pure transformations, and neither is memoized.
variants.code_sketch:
fib = Enumerator.new do |y|
  a, b = 0, 1
  loop { y << a; a, b = b, a + b }
end

10.times { print fib.next, " " }     # one element per pull, infinite source
pitfalls: next raises StopIteration at the end, and mixing it with regular loop/break handling turns normal termination into an error unless it is caught.
An external enumerator is a mutable cursor: rewind only works for rewindable sources (arrays/ranges), and a partially consumed one shared between callers interleaves their elements.
Holding the enumerator retains the producer block and everything it closed over, and the underlying resource is only released when the block finishes or the enumerator is collected.
